blocks.text: Cleaning fixes problems you have already noticed by inspecting data. Validation is the shift from REACTIVELY fixing problems you happen to spot, to PROACTIVELY defining rules that catch problems automatically, every time, even ones you never thought to look for by hand.

Validation defines explicit rules up front, like "age must be between 0 and 120" or "email must contain an @ symbol", and checks every row against them automatically. This catches issues you might never have spotted manually, and catches them again automatically on every new batch of data that arrives later.

blocks.text: Validating incoming data continuously, as part of a pipeline, rather than as a one time manual check, is what makes validation genuinely useful in production. This idea is developed further in the sibling Data Quality Rules and Cleaning Pipelines topics.

blocks.title: Dedicated tools exist
blocks.content: Libraries like pandera and great_expectations formalize this exact pattern for production systems, letting you declare a schema of validation rules once and run it against every new batch of data automatically.

blocks.text: 6. Why Silently Accepting Invalid Data Is Dangerous

A single corrupted row that violates a business rule can cascade into wrong aggregate statistics or a wrong model prediction. Failing loudly and early with a clear validation error is almost always better than a silent wrong answer downstream.

items: Writing rules that are too strict and reject legitimate edge cases.
Writing rules that are too loose and let real problems through.
Treating validation as a one time exercise rather than something that runs on every new batch of data.
Define type, range, format, uniqueness, referential, and consistency rules explicitly.
Run validation automatically on every new batch of data, not just once.
Produce a clear report of which rows failed which rule.
Fail loudly on serious violations rather than silently proceeding.
